• Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR, because a little creatinine is secreted

• PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely in one pass, so its clearance gives the effective renal plasma flow
• Renal blood flow = renal plasma flow ÷ (1 − haematocrit)
• Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ RPF, normally about 20%
• A stone blocking the ureter raises Bowman space pressure, so GFR falls
• High plasma protein (myeloma) raises oncotic pressure: GFR falls while RPF is unchanged
• Afferent constriction (NSAIDs remove the dilating prostaglandins): GFR and RPF both fall
• Efferent constriction (angiotensin II): GFR rises, RPF falls, filtration fraction rises
• An ACE inhibitor can raise creatinine by up to about 30%; a bigger jump suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis

topics.h: Loop of Henle and Bartter syndrome
b: • Thin descending limb: permeable to water only, so the fluid concentrates on the way down
• Thick ascending limb: reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺ through NKCC2, but no water
• NKCC2 carries 1 Na⁺, 1 K⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ into the cell
• K⁺ leaks back out through ROMK, leaving the lumen positive; that charge pushes Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ between the cells
• Fluid leaving the thick ascending limb is hypotonic: the first diluting segment
• The thick ascending limb makes uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), the matrix of every cast
• Defect in NKCC2, ROMK or the chloride channels of the thick ascending limb
• Picture: hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, high renin and aldosterone, normal blood pressure
• Urine calcium is high, because the loop is where calcium was being reclaimed (the opposite of Gitelman)

topics.h: Distal tubule, collecting duct, Gitelman and Liddle
b: • Reabsorbs 5 to 10% of filtered Na⁺ through NCC and stays impermeable to water
• Principal cells: ENaC takes Na⁺ in while ROMK secretes K⁺
• Aldosterone acts on an intracellular receptor to make more ENaC, ROMK and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
• ADH binds V2 receptors and inserts aquaporin 2 into the luminal membrane
• Alpha-intercalated cells secrete H⁺; beta-intercalated cells secrete HCO₃⁻
• Gitelman: NCC defect with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis and hypocalciuria
• Liddle: ENaC stuck on, so hypertension with hypokalaemia and low renin and aldosterone
• Liddle responds to amiloride; spironolactone fails because aldosterone is not driving it
• Apparent mineralocorticoid excess: 11β-HSD2 is missing or blocked by liquorice, so cortisol switches on the aldosterone receptor

b: • Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻): normal about 8 to 12 mEq/L
• Low albumin hides a gap: add about 2.5 mEq/L for each 1 g/dL that albumin sits below 4
High gap: an unmeasured acid has been added:
• Methanol: formic acid damages the optic nerve; give fomepizole
• Ethylene glycol: oxalic acid forms calcium oxalate crystals and causes acute kidney injury
• Salicylates: an early respiratory alkalosis, then a high anion gap acidosis
• Lactic acidosis: shock, sepsis, ischaemia, metformin and cyanide poisoning
• An osmolar gap over 10 mOsm/kg with a high anion gap points to methanol or ethylene glycol
Normal gap: bicarbonate lost, chloride up:
• Diarrhoea: the urine anion gap is negative, because the kidney excretes plenty of NH₄Cl
• Renal tubular acidosis: the urine anion gap is positive, because NH₄⁺ excretion fails
• Litres of normal saline cause a hyperchloraemic acidosis

path.t: Low pressure at the kidney: the fight-back
l: **Low perfusion pressure**, sympathetic **β1** drive or **low NaCl** at the macula densa → juxtaglomerular cells release **renin** → angiotensinogen becomes angiotensin I → **ACE** in the lungs makes **angiotensin II**
Angiotensin II **squeezes the efferent arteriole** → glomerular pressure holds → **GFR is protected** while renal plasma flow falls → filtration fraction rises
Angiotensin II releases **aldosterone** (Na⁺ in, K⁺ and H⁺ out), **ADH** (water in) and **thirst** → volume and pressure climb back → the trigger switches itself off
Block the chain with an **ACE inhibitor** in a kidney that depended on it (bilateral renal artery stenosis) → the efferent relaxes → **GFR collapses**

path.t: How the medulla gets salty and urine gets concentrated
l: The **thick ascending limb** pumps NaCl out with NKCC2 but **lets no water follow** → the surrounding medulla becomes salty → the fluid left inside becomes dilute
The **thin descending limb** passes through that salty medulla → water leaves through aquaporin 1 → fluid concentrates on the way down → the loop **multiplies** the gradient
**ADH** opens aquaporin 2 in the collecting duct and **urea channels** deep in the medulla → water follows the gradient out → urine reaches up to about 1200 mOsm/kg
**Loop diuretics** wash the gradient out → the kidney can neither concentrate nor fully dilute → large volumes of isotonic-ish urine
Vomiting removes **HCl** → **HCO₃⁻ is left behind** → metabolic alkalosis is generated
Vomiting also removes **volume** → **aldosterone and angiotensin II** rise → the kidney's first priority becomes holding sodium
Chloride is too scarce to go back with sodium → sodium is reclaimed **in exchange for H⁺ and K⁺** → **acidic urine** and **hypokalaemia** despite alkalaemia
Give **saline with potassium chloride** → volume and chloride return → aldosterone falls → the kidney can finally dump HCO₃⁻ and the alkalosis corrects
In **acidaemia**, H⁺ moves into cells to be buffered → K⁺ moves **out** to balance the charge → serum K⁺ **rises** (strongest with mineral acids, weaker with organic acids)
In **alkalaemia**, H⁺ leaves cells → K⁺ moves **in** → serum K⁺ **falls**
**Insulin** and **β2 agonists** switch on the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → K⁺ moves into cells → the quick fixes for hyperkalaemia
**Insulin lack** in DKA plus **hyperosmolality** drag K⁺ out of cells → serum K⁺ looks high while the **osmotic diuresis** empties body stores

path.t: Nephritic leaks cells; nephrotic leaks protein
l: **Nephritic**: immune attack **inflames** the glomerular capillaries → the wall breaks → **red cells** escape and set into **RBC casts** → GFR falls → salt and water retained → **hypertension and oedema**
**Nephrotic**: the **podocyte** is injured without much inflammation → the charge and size barrier fails → **over 3.5 g of protein a day** leaks → albumin falls → **oedema**
Low oncotic pressure tells the liver to make more protein → **lipoproteins rise** → fatty casts and Maltese crosses in the urine
Proteins that leak include **antithrombin III** (→ clots, renal vein thrombosis) and **immunoglobulins** (→ infections)
**Shock, sepsis or nephrotoxins** (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin, cisplatin) → the **PCT and thick ascending limb**, the busiest segments, run out of ATP first
Tubular cells **lose polarity and die** → they **slough** into the lumen → they clump into **muddy brown granular casts**
Casts **block** the tubule and filtrate **leaks back** → GFR falls → **oliguria, hyperkalaemia and acidosis**
Dead tubules cannot reclaim sodium or concentrate → **FENa over 2%** and **urine osmolality under 350** → weeks later the tubule regrows → **polyuric recovery** with low potassium
Fewer nephrons → **phosphate retained** → **FGF23** rises to push phosphate out → FGF23 **inhibits 1α-hydroxylase**
Less **calcitriol** → less calcium absorbed from the gut → **serum calcium falls** while phosphate binds what calcium is left
Low calcium, high phosphate and low calcitriol → the parathyroids grow → **secondary hyperparathyroidism** → bone is resorbed → **osteitis fibrosa cystica** (renal osteodystrophy)
Years later the glands act on their own → **tertiary hyperparathyroidism** → calcium now runs **high**
A stone forms when urine is **supersaturated**: too much solute (**calcium, oxalate, urate, cystine**) or too little water
**Urine pH** chooses the stone: **alkaline** urine favours calcium phosphate and struvite; **acidic** urine favours uric acid and cystine
**Citrate** binds calcium and protects against stones → low citrate in **distal RTA** and chronic acidosis invites calcium stones
**Fat malabsorption** (Crohn disease, ileal resection) lets fat grab gut calcium → oxalate is left free → absorbed in the colon → **calcium oxalate stones**
Any diuretic acting **before** the collecting duct (acetazolamide, loops, thiazides) sends **more Na⁺** to the principal cells
More Na⁺ through **ENaC** → the lumen turns more negative → **K⁺ is pulled out** through ROMK
Volume falls → **aldosterone** rises → even more ENaC and ROMK → more K⁺ and H⁺ lost → **hypokalaemia with alkalosis**
Diuretics acting **at** the collecting duct (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) block this step → they **spare potassium** and can cause hyperkalaemia

q.s: A 58-year-old man with hypertension comes to the emergency department because of severe pain and swelling of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint that began overnight. Three weeks ago, a new antihypertensive drug was added to his regimen. Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. His serum calcium is at the upper limit of normal, and his fasting glucose has risen since his last visit.
q.w: Thiazides compete with urate for the organic anion transporter in the proximal tubule and cause volume contraction, which increases urate reabsorption. Hyperuricaemia precipitates gout, and the same class raises calcium and glucose.
q.f: Ototoxicity and low calcium instead → a loop diuretic
q.ql: Which of the following drugs was most likely added three weeks ago?

c: serum calcium is at the upper limit of normal
tm.m: Thiazide → volume contraction and competition for urate secretion → serum urate rises → crystals form in a cool distal joint → gout
tm.g: Gout plus high calcium plus high glucose after a new antihypertensive is the thiazide signature
f: the new drug had caused ankle swelling and flushing
the new drug had caused a dry cough and a raised potassium
the new drug had slightly lowered his urate
the new drug had caused breast enlargement and a raised potassium
x: Causes peripheral oedema and flushing, not hyperuricaemia
Causes cough, angioedema and hyperkalaemia; it does not raise urate or calcium
Mildly uricosuric, so it lowers urate rather than provoking gout
Causes hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia; calcium and glucose are unaffected

q.s: A 67-year-old woman is admitted with pyelonephritis and decompensated heart failure. She is treated with intravenous gentamicin and high-dose intravenous furosemide. On day 5, she reports ringing in both ears and difficulty following conversation. Her serum creatinine is unchanged from admission. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes.
o: Blockade of carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
Blockade of epithelial sodium channels in the cochlea
Blockade of Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransport in the stria vascularis
Free radical injury to outer hair cells
Osmotic shift of water out of the endolymph
q.w: Loop diuretics block NKCC1 in the stria vascularis, the pump that builds the potassium-rich endolymph that powers hearing. The effect is dose-related and far worse alongside an aminoglycoside, whose own toxicity is free radical injury to hair cells.
q.f: Asked about the aminoglycoside instead → free radical injury to outer hair cells
q.ql: Which of the following best explains how the diuretic contributes to her symptoms?

tm.m: High-dose loop diuretic → NKCC1 blocked in the stria vascularis → endolymph loses K⁺ and its charge → hair cells cannot transduce → tinnitus and hearing loss
tm.g: Loops plus aminoglycosides are the classic ototoxic pair; the loop's share is the stria vascularis pump
f: the drug had been acetazolamide given for glaucoma
the drug had been amiloride given for lithium-induced diabetes insipidus
the question asked how gentamicin damages hearing
the drug had been mannitol given for raised intracranial pressure
x: How acetazolamide lowers eye pressure; it has nothing to do with hearing
Amiloride blocks ENaC in the collecting duct and is not ototoxic
The aminoglycoside's own mechanism, not the diuretic's
Describes an osmotic agent such as mannitol, not furosemide

q.s: A 26-year-old woman plans to climb a 5,800-meter peak next month. On earlier treks above 3,000 meters, she developed headache, nausea, and insomnia. Her physician prescribes a drug to start the day before the ascent to prevent these symptoms. She has no other medical conditions.
q.w: Acetazolamide blocks proximal carbonic anhydrase, so filtered HCO₃⁻ escapes into the urine (alkaline urine) and chloride is kept: a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. The acidosis drives breathing, which offsets the hypoxic alkalosis of altitude.
q.f: Severe diarrhoea instead → the same acidosis but an acidic urine
q.ql: Which of the following sets of changes is most likely once she starts the drug?

tm.m: Carbonic anhydrase blocked → filtered HCO₃⁻ cannot be reclaimed → alkaline urine and falling serum HCO₃⁻ → Cl⁻ retained → acidosis stimulates ventilation
tm.g: Acetazolamide makes a normal anion gap acidosis with an alkaline urine
f: she had swallowed large doses of sodium bicarbonate
she had been vomiting for three days and was volume depleted
she had severe diarrhoea instead, with kidneys that work
she had diabetic ketoacidosis
x: A bicarbonate load, which the kidney dumps into the urine
Volume-depleted metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
Diarrhoea: the gut loses HCO₃⁻ and the healthy kidney acidifies the urine
A high anion gap acidosis such as ketoacidosis, where an unmeasured anion replaces HCO₃⁻

q.s: A 61-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has been taking furosemide, lisinopril, carvedilol, and a fourth drug added to reduce mortality. Six months later, he reports painful enlargement of both breasts. His serum potassium is 5.3 mEq/L. His physician wants to keep the survival benefit while removing this adverse effect.
q.w: Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors and raises oestrogen activity, causing gynaecomastia. Eplerenone is a more selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with the same mortality benefit in heart failure and far less gynaecomastia.
q.f: No heart failure, just a need to spare potassium → amiloride
q.ql: Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement for the fourth drug?

c: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
tm.m: Spironolactone → blocks androgen receptors as well as aldosterone receptors → relative oestrogen excess → gynaecomastia → swap to a selective blocker
tm.g: Keep aldosterone blockade, lose the antiandrogen: eplerenone
f: he only needed to stop losing potassium on furosemide, with no mortality goal
he needed better blood pressure control with no heart failure
his physician wanted to keep the same drug and accept a smaller benefit
he needed a potassium-sparing drug and could not take amiloride
x: Spares potassium by blocking ENaC but carries no proven survival benefit in heart failure
Not a mortality drug in heart failure, and it does not block aldosterone
Gynaecomastia can persist; switching to the selective drug is the answer
Another ENaC blocker with no survival benefit, and it can cause kidney stones

q.s: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for hypertension found at a sports physical. His blood pressure is 162/98 mm Hg. His father and an uncle developed hypertension as teenagers. Examination is otherwise normal. He takes no medications and denies licorice or supplement use.
o: Gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel
Loss-of-function mutation in the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter
q.w: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation in ENaC. The channel reabsorbs sodium without aldosterone, so volume expands, renin and aldosterone are suppressed, and potassium and hydrogen are lost. Amiloride, not spironolactone, treats it.
q.f: Same labs after eating licorice → apparent mineralocorticoid excess

c: father and an uncle developed hypertension as teenagers
tm.m: ENaC stuck open → Na⁺ reabsorbed without aldosterone → volume expands → renin and aldosterone switch off → K⁺ and H⁺ secreted → hypokalaemic alkalosis
tm.g: Hypertension, hypokalaemia, low renin and LOW aldosterone in a family = Liddle
f: aldosterone had been high with low renin
he had been eating large amounts of black licorice
renin and aldosterone had both been high in a young woman with a renal bruit
his blood pressure had been low with low urine calcium
x: Aldosterone would be high, not low
Fits the labs, but he denies licorice and the family pattern points to an inherited channel
Renal artery narrowing raises renin and aldosterone
Gitelman syndrome causes low or normal blood pressure

q.s: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for poor growth, salt craving, and frequent urination. Her blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. She takes no medications, and there is no history of vomiting or laxative use. Renal ultrasonography shows medullary nephrocalcinosis.
q.w: Bartter syndrome impairs NKCC2 or its partner channels in the thick ascending limb, mimicking a loop diuretic: salt wasting, high renin and aldosterone, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis. Blood pressure stays normal or low.

tm.m: NKCC2 fails → salt wasted → renin and aldosterone rise → K⁺ and H⁺ secreted distally → lumen-positive charge lost so Ca²⁺ is not reclaimed → hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
tm.g: Hypokalaemic alkalosis with normal BP: urine calcium high means loop (Bartter), low means DCT (Gitelman)
f: she had hypertension with low renin and low aldosterone
urine calcium had been low with low magnesium in a young adult
she had glucosuria, aminoaciduria and phosphaturia with acidosis
the question asked where water leaves while salt stays in the tubule

Gitelman syndrome, which causes hypocalciuria and low magnesium
Fanconi syndrome gives a proximal RTA with acidosis, not alkalosis
Moves water only and has no inherited salt-wasting syndrome

q.s: A 24-year-old woman has muscle cramps and fatigue. She has no vomiting or diarrhea and takes no medications. Blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. A urine drug screen for diuretics is negative.
q.w: Gitelman syndrome is an inherited loss of the thiazide-sensitive NCC in the distal convoluted tubule. Like a thiazide, it wastes salt and magnesium, keeps calcium (hypocalciuria) and produces a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with a high urine chloride.
