tm.m: NCC lost → Na⁺ and Cl⁻ wasted → aldosterone rises → K⁺ and H⁺ secreted → alkalosis; Mg²⁺ channel downregulated → low Mg²⁺; calcium reabsorption enhanced → hypocalciuria
tm.g: Low urine calcium plus low magnesium in a hypokalaemic alkalosis = thiazide look-alike
f: she had a normal anion gap acidosis with alkaline urine
she had hyperkalaemia and the drug blocked ENaC
urine calcium had been high with nephrocalcinosis
she had hyperkalaemia with a mild acidosis
x: Causes a normal anion gap acidosis, not an alkalosis
Spares potassium; it would raise potassium, not lower it
Mimics Bartter syndrome, with high urine calcium
Causes hyperkalaemia and acidosis

q.s: A 54-year-old man has new hypertension and leg weakness. He started a herbal remedy for heartburn two months ago and has been eating large amounts of a black candy. Blood pressure is 168/100 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and bicarbonate is 32 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity and serum aldosterone are both low.
q.w: Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice blocks 11β-HSD2 in the collecting duct. That enzyme normally converts cortisol to cortisone so cortisol cannot reach the mineralocorticoid receptor. Unchecked, cortisol acts like aldosterone: hypertension, hypokalaemia, alkalosis, with renin and aldosterone suppressed.
q.f: Ambiguous genitalia and salt wasting in a newborn → 21-hydroxylase
q.ql: Inhibition of which of the following enzymes best explains these findings?

c: large amounts of a black candy
renin activity and serum aldosterone are both low
tm.m: Licorice → 11β-HSD2 blocked → cortisol stays active in principal cells → mineralocorticoid receptor switched on → Na⁺ retained, K⁺ and H⁺ lost → renin and aldosterone suppressed
tm.g: Mineralocorticoid excess with LOW aldosterone: something else is hitting the receptor
f: a girl had hypertension, hypokalaemia and virilisation
a teenager had hypertension, hypokalaemia and no puberty
a newborn girl had ambiguous genitalia and salt wasting
he had salt wasting and hyperkalaemia with normal cortisol
x: Deficiency raises 11-deoxycorticosterone and androgens: hypertension with virilisation
Deficiency causes hypertension with absent sex hormones in a teenager
Deficiency causes salt wasting and virilisation, not hypertension
Deficiency causes salt wasting and hyperkalaemia

q.s: A 64-year-old man who smokes 2 packs of cigarettes daily has 3 weeks of cough and confusion. He is euvolemic on examination and takes no medications. Chest x-ray shows a central hilar mass.
q.w: Small cell lung cancer secretes ADH ectopically. Water is retained despite low serum osmolality, so the urine is inappropriately concentrated, the patient stays euvolaemic (aldosterone falls and natriuresis follows) and urine sodium is high. Thyroid function is normal.
q.f: Very dilute urine and huge water intake → excess water intake (primary polydipsia)
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?

tm.m: Tumour makes ADH → aquaporin 2 inserted → free water reabsorbed → serum diluted → volume sensors trigger natriuresis → euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine
tm.g: Low serum osmolality with urine osmolality above it, in a euvolaemic smoker = SIADH
f: he had a subarachnoid hemorrhage, low volume and high urine sodium
urine osmolality had been 60 mOsm/kg in a man drinking 8 liters a day
he had been vomiting, with dry mucosa and urine sodium 8 mEq/L
serum osmolality had been normal with a milky serum
x: Follows brain injury and leaves the patient volume depleted
Produces maximally dilute urine, not urine osmolality of 540
Urine sodium would be low and the patient dry
Serum osmolality would be normal

q.s: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has had increasing thirst and urination for 6 months. She has taken the same mood stabilizer for 10 years. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L. During a water deprivation test, urine osmolality stays at 160 mOsm/kg and does not rise after an injection of desmopressin.
o: Excess ADH release from the hypothalamus
Reduced aquaporin 2 response to ADH in the collecting duct
Reduced water permeability of the thin descending limb
q.w: Long-term lithium enters principal cells through ENaC and blunts V2 signalling, so aquaporin 2 is not inserted: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Urine stays dilute through water deprivation and does not respond to desmopressin. Amiloride, which blocks lithium entry, helps.
q.f: Urine concentrates after desmopressin → destruction of the posterior pituitary (central DI)
q.ql: Which of the following best explains her findings?

c: does not rise after an injection of desmopressin
tm.m: Lithium enters via ENaC → V2 signal blunted → aquaporin 2 not inserted → free water lost → serum sodium rises → thirst
tm.g: Dilute urine that ignores desmopressin = nephrogenic DI; lithium is the classic cause
f: urine osmolality had doubled after desmopressin following head trauma
she had concentrated urine and a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L
the question asked where water leaves the nephron without salt
she had high sodium with no thirst after a hypothalamic stroke
x: Central DI responds to desmopressin
SIADH gives concentrated urine and hyponatraemia
Aquaporin 1 there is not the lithium target and does not depend on ADH
Adipsia would not explain urine that ignores desmopressin

q.s: A 58-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder is admitted with a serum sodium of 106 mEq/L after 2 weeks of drinking beer and eating little. Hypertonic saline raises her sodium to 128 mEq/L within 24 hours. Three days later, she develops dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and weakness of all four limbs.
q.w: Correcting chronic hyponatraemia faster than about 8 to 10 mEq/L a day shrinks brain cells that had adapted to low osmolality, and the central pons demyelinates (osmotic demyelination). Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts give quadriparesis, dysarthria and dysphagia, sometimes locked-in syndrome.
q.f: Confusion, ataxia and eye palsy from thiamine lack → mammillary bodies
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion causing her new symptoms?

c: dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and weakness of all four limbs
tm.m: Brain adapts to low sodium by losing osmolytes → sodium raised too fast → water leaves cells → oligodendrocytes in the pons injured → demyelination of corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts
tm.g: Low to high, the pons will die: a rise of 22 in a day is far too fast
f: she had a wide-based gait from chronic alcohol use
she had confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia without thiamine
she had bitemporal hemianopia
she had contralateral sensory loss followed by burning pain
x: Alcohol-related truncal ataxia, not quadriparesis
Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency
Visual field loss, not corticobulbar signs
Thalamic syndrome gives sensory loss and pain

q.s: A 72-year-old man with chronic kidney disease feels weak after starting a new antihypertensive drug. His pulse is 54/min and irregular. An ECG shows peaked T waves and widening of the QRS complex.
q.w: Once hyperkalaemia changes the ECG, intravenous calcium comes first: it raises the threshold potential and stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes. It does not lower potassium, so insulin with dextrose, albuterol and removal (binders, diuretics, dialysis) follow.
q.f: Same potassium with a normal ECG → insulin with dextrose first
q.ql: Which of the following is the most appropriate first drug?

c: peaked T waves and widening of the QRS complex
tm.m: High K⁺ → resting potential less negative → sodium channels inactivate → slow conduction and arrhythmia risk → calcium restores the gap to threshold
tm.g: ECG changes = protect the heart first (calcium), then shift, then remove
f: he had no IV access and needed a quick shift
the ECG had been normal and the goal was to shift potassium into cells fast
he was stable and needed potassium removed from the body over hours
he had severe metabolic acidosis as the cause
x: Shifts K⁺ into cells but does not protect the heart
Lowers K⁺ within 15 to 30 minutes, but the heart needs protecting first
Takes hours and removes K⁺ slowly
Helps mainly when acidosis is driving the hyperkalaemia

q.s: A 49-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder has fatigue and muscle weakness. Despite 3 days of intravenous potassium chloride, her serum potassium remains low. She takes omeprazole daily. An ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves.
q.w: Intracellular magnesium normally plugs ROMK channels in the distal nephron. With low magnesium the plug is gone, so potassium keeps leaking into the urine whatever is infused. Low magnesium also blunts PTH release and action, which explains the low calcium. Replace magnesium first.
q.f: Low phosphate after refeeding instead → phosphate
q.ql: Correcting which of the following is most likely to allow her potassium to normalize?

c: Despite 3 days of intravenous potassium chloride
tm.m: Alcohol and PPI → low Mg²⁺ → ROMK unplugged in principal cells → K⁺ wasted in urine → potassium will not correct; low Mg²⁺ also cuts PTH → low calcium
tm.g: Potassium that will not stay up: check and replace magnesium
f: she had tetany with normal magnesium after thyroid surgery
she had a hypochloraemic alkalosis from vomiting maintaining the losses
she had heart failure and respiratory failure after starting feeds
she had confusion, ataxia and nystagmus
x: Low calcium here follows the low magnesium; it does not drive potassium loss
Matters in vomiting-related alkalosis, but she has already received potassium chloride
Low phosphate weakens muscle but does not keep potassium leaking
Needed in alcohol use disorder for Wernicke, not for potassium balance

q.s: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with abdominal pain, vomiting, and deep, rapid breathing. Blood glucose is 610 mg/dL, serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L, and arterial pH is 7.08. Intravenous fluids and an insulin infusion are started.
o: High serum potassium with depleted total body potassium
High serum potassium with increased total body potassium
High serum potassium with normal total body potassium
Low serum potassium with depleted total body potassium
Normal serum potassium with increased total body potassium
q.w: Insulin lack and hyperosmolality shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium reads high, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting have drained the body's stores. Insulin drives potassium back into cells and serum levels can crash, so potassium is replaced once it falls below about 5.3 mEq/L.
q.f: After 6 hours of insulin without replacement → low serum, depleted stores
q.ql: Which of the following best describes his potassium status before treatment?

tm.m: No insulin plus hyperosmolality → K⁺ leaves cells → serum K⁺ high → osmotic diuresis and vomiting wash K⁺ out → body stores fall → insulin unmasks the deficit
tm.g: In DKA the serum potassium lies: total body potassium is low
f: he had advanced kidney failure and was eating bananas
the sample had been haemolysed in a healthy man
he had received several hours of insulin with no potassium added
he had potassium supplements with kidney failure but a normal level that morning
x: Fits kidney failure with intake, not osmotic diuresis
A shift alone, such as a haemolysed sample, would not drain stores
What appears after insulin starts without replacement
Does not match a serum potassium of 5.8

q.s: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after drinking a sweet-tasting liquid from a container in his garage. He is drowsy and slurring his words. Pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 28/min and deep. Urinalysis shows envelope-shaped crystals.
q.w: Anion gap = 140 − (101 + 9) = 30. Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 90/18 + 14/2.8 = 280 + 5 + 5 = 290, so the osmolar gap is 325 − 290 = 35. Both gaps high with oxalate crystals: ethylene glycol. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.
q.f: Hours later, once the glycol is metabolised → the osmolar gap shrinks while the anion gap stays
q.ql: Which of the following is the anion gap and the osmolar gap?

tm.m: Ethylene glycol is an osmole → osmolar gap; alcohol dehydrogenase turns it into glycolic and oxalic acid → anion gap acidosis → calcium oxalate crystals → AKI
tm.g: High anion gap plus high osmolar gap = toxic alcohol until proven otherwise
f: he had pure diarrhoea with no ingestion
he had drunk a large amount of ethanol with no acidosis
his bicarbonate had been 18 mEq/L with the same osmolality
he had DKA with a normal measured osmolality gap
x: Both gaps are clearly raised here
An osmolar gap with no acidosis suggests ethanol or isopropyl alcohol
Uses the wrong bicarbonate: 140 − (101 + 9) is 30
Ignores the measured osmolality of 325

q.s: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 12 hours after drinking homemade liquor. He reports blurred vision and says it looks like he is in a snowstorm. Pupils are dilated and poorly reactive. Arterial pH is 7.12 with a high anion gap and a high osmolar gap.
o: Binding of formate as a stable complex
Chelation of the alcohol in plasma
q.w: Methanol itself is fairly harmless; alcohol dehydrogenase turns it into formaldehyde and then formic acid, which poisons the optic nerve and causes the acidosis. Fomepizole competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase so the parent compound is excreted or dialysed before it is converted.
q.f: Flushing and vomiting after alcohol on metronidazole → that blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase
q.ql: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most appropriate antidote?

c: high anion gap and a high osmolar gap
tm.m: Methanol → alcohol dehydrogenase → formaldehyde → formic acid → mitochondrial poisoning of the optic nerve and anion gap acidosis
tm.g: Toxic alcohols harm only after alcohol dehydrogenase: block that enzyme
f: the question asked how disulfiram makes drinkers feel ill
the treatment had been folinic acid to speed formate clearance
the poison had been lead and the antidote succimer
the question asked which enzyme chronic alcohol use induces
x: Disulfiram inhibits this enzyme; no antidote activates it
Folate helps clear formate metabolically; nothing binds it
Chelators bind metals, not alcohols
Not the main route of methanol toxicity

q.s: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after taking a large number of pills. She has tinnitus, vomiting, and a temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F). Respirations are 32/min and deep.
o: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis
q.w: Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre directly (respiratory alkalosis) and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation (lactic and keto acids: high anion gap acidosis). Anion gap = 140 − (102 + 14) = 24. Winter predicts a PaCO₂ of 27 to 31 for a bicarbonate of 14; 21 is lower, so a second, respiratory process is present.
q.f: PaCO₂ of 29 instead → metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
q.ql: Which of the following best describes her acid-base status?

tm.m: Aspirin → respiratory centre stimulated → CO₂ blown off; aspirin → uncoupled mitochondria → lactate and ketoacids → anion gap acidosis → pH lands near normal
tm.g: Near-normal pH with both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ very low = two disorders; with tinnitus think salicylate
f: she had a bicarbonate of 18 after 3 days at high altitude with no ingestion
PaCO₂ had been 29 mm Hg
the anion gap had been 10 with a bicarbonate of 14
she had been vomiting with a bicarbonate of 34 and hyperventilating from pain
x: The anion gap of 24 shows an added acid
PaCO₂ is below the Winter range
The gap is 24
Bicarbonate is low, not high

q.s: A 4-week-old boy has had 5 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit contains no bile. He is dehydrated, and a firm, mobile mass is palpable in the epigastrium. Urinalysis shows acidic urine.
o: Excess bicarbonate secretion by beta-intercalated cells
Gastric acid absorbed into the blood
Impaired H⁺ secretion in the distal tubule
Sodium reabsorption in exchange for H⁺ to defend volume
q.w: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes loss of HCl. Volume depletion raises aldosterone, and chloride is too low to accompany sodium, so the collecting duct reclaims sodium in exchange for H⁺ and K⁺. The result is paradoxical aciduria despite a metabolic alkalosis.
q.f: Early, before he was dry → alkaline urine as excess HCO₃⁻ is dumped
q.ql: Which of the following best explains his acidic urine?

tm.m: HCl vomited → alkalosis and volume loss → aldosterone up, Cl⁻ low → Na⁺ reclaimed with H⁺ and K⁺ secreted → acidic urine and hypokalaemia keep the alkalosis going
tm.g: Volume beats pH: the kidney defends volume first, so urine turns acidic in a vomiting alkalosis
f: the question asked how the kidney would correct the alkalosis once volume and chloride are restored
the question asked about hydrogen ions that were swallowed back
he had a distal RTA with acidosis and alkaline urine
he had been given acetazolamide
x: That would make the urine alkaline; it happens once chloride is replaced
The acid is lost, which is why he is alkalotic
Type 1 RTA gives acidosis with alkaline urine
Acetazolamide causes acidosis with alkaline urine

q.s: A 36-year-old woman has fatigue and muscle cramps. Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. She has dental erosions and calluses on the backs of her fingers, but she denies vomiting. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and bicarbonate is 33 mEq/L.
q.w: Low urine chloride (under 20 mEq/L) marks a saline-responsive alkalosis from chloride loss outside the kidney: vomiting or nasogastric suction. Dental erosions and knuckle calluses point to self-induced vomiting. Diuretics and Bartter or Gitelman keep urine chloride high, and hyperaldosteronism raises blood pressure.
q.f: Urine chloride 70 with normal BP → current diuretic use
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her metabolic alkalosis?

c: calluses on the backs of her fingers
tm.m: Vomiting → HCl and volume lost → aldosterone up, Cl⁻ scarce → H⁺ and K⁺ secreted → alkalosis maintained; kidney holds every Cl⁻ → urine Cl⁻ very low
tm.g: Urine chloride under 20 = the chloride left by the mouth or gut, not the kidney
f: urine chloride had been high with high urine calcium in a child
urine chloride had been 70 mEq/L with a positive diuretic screen
urine chloride had been high with low urine calcium and low magnesium, screen negative
she had hypertension, low renin and high aldosterone
x: Urine chloride would be high, as with a loop diuretic
Urine chloride stays high while the diuretic acts
Urine chloride would be high
Causes hypertension and a saline-resistant, high urine chloride alkalosis

q.s: A 68-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes for a routine visit. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and is at his usual level of breathlessness. He is alert and oriented.
o: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
q.w: PaCO₂ is 20 above 40. Acute retention would raise bicarbonate only about 2 (1 per 10 mm Hg); after 3 to 5 days the kidney adds about 3.5 per 10, predicting 31. A bicarbonate of 32 with pH 7.35 fits a stable chronic respiratory acidosis.
q.f: Same PaCO₂ with bicarbonate 26 and pH 7.24 → acute respiratory acidosis
q.ql: Which of the following best describes his acid-base status?

tm.m: Chronic CO₂ retention → renal tubules sense acidosis → more H⁺ secreted and HCO₃⁻ generated over days → bicarbonate rises by 3.5 per 10 mm Hg → pH pulled back toward normal
tm.g: Expected bicarbonate tells acute from chronic: 1 per 10 versus 3.5 per 10
f: bicarbonate had been 26 with a pH of 7.24 after an opioid overdose
he had been vomiting with PaCO₂ 50 and bicarbonate 38 and pH 7.49
bicarbonate had been 20 with a pH of 7.10 during septic shock
bicarbonate had been 40 after starting high-dose diuretics
x: Bicarbonate would be about 26, not 32
The pH is low, so the primary process is an acidosis
Bicarbonate is high, not low
Bicarbonate fits the predicted 31 within about 2

q.s: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a panic attack. She has tingling around her mouth and in her fingers, and her hands cramp into flexion when a blood pressure cuff is inflated. Respirations are 30/min. Arterial pH is 7.55 and PaCO₂ is 24 mm Hg.
o: Decreased total serum calcium from renal losses
Increased binding of calcium to albumin
q.w: Hyperventilation removes CO₂ and raises pH. Albumin releases H⁺ in alkalaemia, exposing negative sites that bind more calcium, so ionised calcium falls while total calcium is unchanged. Low ionised calcium makes nerves fire: perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm and a positive Trousseau sign.
q.f: Same signs after thyroid surgery → reduced parathyroid hormone release
q.ql: Which of the following best explains her tingling and cramping?

c: hands cramp into flexion when a blood pressure cuff is inflated
tm.m: Hyperventilation → CO₂ falls → pH rises → albumin gives up H⁺ → binds more Ca²⁺ → ionised Ca²⁺ falls → nerve membranes excitable → tetany
tm.g: Total calcium normal, ionised calcium low: alkalosis moves calcium onto albumin
f: she had been taking a loop diuretic for weeks
the question asked which hormone a medullary thyroid cancer secretes
she had chronic kidney disease with high phosphate
she had the same signs a day after a total thyroidectomy
x: Minutes of hyperventilation do not change total calcium
Calcitonin has little effect on serum calcium in adults
Phosphate is not raised by panic
Her parathyroid glands are intact

q.s: A 44-year-old woman with dry eyes and dry mouth for 3 years has flank pain. CT shows a calcium phosphate stone in the left ureter and medullary nephrocalcinosis. Urine pH is 6.4.
o: Excess bicarbonate loss in the proximal tubule
Impaired ammonia production from aldosterone deficiency
Impaired H⁺ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells
Increased chloride reabsorption in the loop
q.w: Sjögren syndrome can cause distal (type 1) RTA: alpha-intercalated cells cannot secrete H⁺, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidaemia. Hypokalaemia, hypercalciuria and low urine citrate encourage calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis. Anion gap = 139 − (112 + 16) = 11, normal.
q.f: Hyperkalaemia with urine pH under 5.5 in a diabetic → type 4 RTA
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

tm.m: Autoimmune injury to alpha-intercalated cells → H⁺ not secreted → urine cannot acidify → HCO₃⁻ falls, Cl⁻ rises → bone buffers release calcium and citrate falls → calcium phosphate stones
tm.g: Normal gap acidosis with urine pH over 5.5, low K⁺ and stones = type 1 RTA
f: she had Fanconi syndrome from myeloma with glucosuria
she had hyperkalaemia, diabetes and urine pH 5.0 on lisinopril
the question asked what replaces lost bicarbonate in a hyperchloraemic acidosis
she had alkalosis with low urine calcium and low magnesium
x: Type 2 RTA can acidify urine below 5.5 once bicarbonate is low, and stones are rare
Type 4 RTA causes hyperkalaemia
Not a recognised cause of RTA
Gitelman syndrome causes alkalosis, not acidosis

q.s: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy was started on lisinopril 2 months ago to reduce proteinuria. He feels well and has had no vomiting or diarrhea. He also takes metformin and atorvastatin. Examination shows mild ankle edema. Urine pH is 5.1.
o: Impaired H⁺-ATPase function in alpha-intercalated cells
Loss of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Reduced ammonium production caused by hyperkalemia
Urinary loss of bicarbonate from Fanconi syndrome
q.w: Type 4 RTA comes from too little aldosterone action: diabetic damage to the juxtaglomerular apparatus (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism) worsened by an ACE inhibitor. Hyperkalaemia suppresses ammoniagenesis in the proximal tubule, so there is too little NH₃ to carry H⁺ out. H⁺ pumps still work, so urine pH stays under 5.5.
q.f: Urine pH over 5.5 with hypokalaemia and stones → impaired H⁺-ATPase function
q.ql: Which of the following most directly limits acid excretion in this patient?

tm.m: Diabetes damages JG cells → little renin → little aldosterone (plus ACE inhibitor) → K⁺ retained → hyperkalaemia blocks ammoniagenesis → less NH₄⁺ excreted → normal gap acidosis with acidic urine
tm.g: Hyperkalaemic normal gap acidosis with acidic urine = type 4: ammonia, not the pump, is the bottleneck
f: urine pH had been 6.5 with hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis
he had started acetazolamide for glaucoma
the question asked about titratable acid in advanced CKD with low GFR
he had glucosuria with normal blood glucose and phosphaturia
x: Type 1 RTA, with urine pH over 5.5 and hypokalaemia
Acetazolamide effect; he is not taking it
Contributes in advanced CKD but does not explain the high potassium
Type 2 RTA causes hypokalaemia

q.s: A 66-year-old man has back pain and fatigue. Serum protein is high with a low albumin, and protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike. Urinalysis shows 2+ glucose with a serum glucose of 94 mg/dL. Serum phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, and he has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
q.w: Light chains filtered in multiple myeloma injure proximal tubule cells, causing Fanconi syndrome: glucose, amino acids, phosphate and bicarbonate escape. Losing bicarbonate is a proximal (type 2) RTA, and the phosphate loss weakens bone.
q.f: Urine pH stuck above 5.5 with stones → collecting duct (type 1 RTA)
q.ql: In which part of the nephron is the transport defect causing his acidosis?

c: 2+ glucose with a serum glucose of 94 mg/dL
tm.m: Myeloma light chains filtered → endocytosed by PCT cells → cell injury → glucose, phosphate, amino acids and HCO₃⁻ lost → normal gap acidosis
tm.g: Glucosuria with normal blood glucose + low phosphate + acidosis = Fanconi = proximal
f: urine pH had stayed above 5.5 with calcium phosphate stones
he had hypokalaemic alkalosis with low urine calcium
he had nephrotic-range proteinuria from AL amyloid
he had hypokalaemic alkalosis with high urine calcium
x: Distal RTA, without glucosuria or phosphaturia
Gitelman-type defects cause alkalosis
Amyloid in the glomerulus causes proteinuria, not bicarbonate wasting
Bartter-type defects cause alkalosis

q.s: A 7-year-old boy has puffy eyes and cola-colored urine. He had crusted, honey-colored sores around his nose 3 weeks ago that resolved. Blood pressure is 132/86 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts and 1+ protein.
o: Basket-weave splitting of the basement membrane
q.w: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows group A strep throat or skin infection by 2 to 3 weeks. Immune complexes deposit beneath the epithelium as humps, complement is consumed (low C3), and children usually recover fully. After skin infection, anti-DNase B is the more reliable antibody.
q.f: Haematuria 2 days after a sore throat with normal C3 → mesangial deposits (IgA)
q.ql: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy?

tm.m: Group A strep antigen → immune complexes → subepithelial deposits → complement activated (low C3) → glomerular inflammation → haematuria, RBC casts, hypertension
tm.g: Weeks after strep, low C3, RBC casts in a child = subepithelial humps
f: he had haematuria, deafness and an affected maternal uncle
he had heavy proteinuria and normal light microscopy after a cold
haematuria had begun 2 days after a sore throat with normal complement
he had hepatitis C and low C3 as an adult
x: Alport syndrome, from type IV collagen mutation
Minimal change disease, which is nephrotic
IgA nephropathy starts within days of infection with normal C3
Membranoproliferative GN

q.s: A 24-year-old man has had three episodes of painless, tea-colored urine over 2 years, each starting the day after an upper respiratory infection. Between episodes his urine shows microscopic hematuria. Blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Serum C3 and C4 are normal.
o: IgG in a linear pattern along the basement membrane
q.w: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide. Poorly galactosylated IgA1 forms complexes that lodge in the mesangium, and episodes of haematuria follow mucosal infections within 1 to 2 days. Complement levels stay normal.
q.f: Haematuria 3 weeks after a sore throat with low C3 → subepithelial humps
q.ql: A kidney biopsy is most likely to show deposits of which immunoglobulin, and where?

c: the day after an upper respiratory infection
tm.m: Mucosal infection → abnormal IgA1 and anti-IgA antibodies → complexes trapped in the mesangium → mesangial cells proliferate → haematuria within days
tm.g: Haematuria a day or two after a cold, normal complement = mesangial IgA
f: the haematuria had begun 3 weeks after strep throat with low C3
he had coughed blood with kidney failure
he had SLE with wire loops on light microscopy
he had a monoclonal IgM paraprotein with hyperviscosity
x: Subepithelial humps belong to poststreptococcal GN, which carries IgG and C3
Anti-GBM disease
Lupus or membranoproliferative GN
Not a recognised pattern for this story

q.s: A 27-year-old man who smokes has had 1 week of coughing up blood and 3 days of reduced urine output. Chest x-ray shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 mg/dL to 4.2 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. Immunofluorescence of a kidney biopsy shows smooth, ribbon-like IgG staining along the capillary loops.
o: Noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of type IV collagen
Type I collagen in the interstitium
q.w: Anti-GBM disease targets the α3 chain of type IV collagen, found in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes: a type II hypersensitivity with linear IgG on immunofluorescence. Smoking and inhaled injury expose the alveolar antigen, giving lung haemorrhage (Goodpasture syndrome). Plasmapheresis removes the antibody.
q.f: Sinusitis, lung nodules and no immune deposits → proteinase 3 (GPA)
q.ql: The antibodies in this patient are directed against which of the following?

c: ribbon-like IgG staining along the capillary loops
tm.m: Antibodies to type IV collagen α3 → bind glomerular and alveolar basement membrane → complement and neutrophils → crescentic GN and lung haemorrhage
tm.g: Lung bleeding + kidney failure + LINEAR IgG = anti-GBM (type IV collagen)
f: he had flaccid mouth blisters with a positive Nikolsky sign
he had nephrotic syndrome with spike and dome basement membrane
he had sinusitis, lung nodules and no immune deposits on biopsy
the question asked what keloids are made from
x: Pemphigus vulgaris, a skin disease
Membranous nephropathy, which is nephrotic
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis gives pauci-immune staining
Not targeted in any glomerulonephritis

q.s: A 19-year-old man has had microscopic hematuria since childhood and now has a rising serum creatinine. He wears hearing aids for bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and slit-lamp examination shows a conical bulge of the anterior lens. His maternal uncle needed dialysis at age 30.
q.w: Alport syndrome is a mutation in type IV collagen, usually X-linked. The glomerular basement membrane thins, then splits into a basket-weave pattern; the cochlea and lens use the same collagen, giving deafness and anterior lenticonus. Affected males progress to kidney failure.
q.f: Lens dislocated upward with tall stature → fibrillin 1
q.ql: A mutation in which of the following is most likely responsible?

c: conical bulge of the anterior lens
tm.m: Faulty type IV collagen → basement membranes of glomerulus, cochlea and lens fail → haematuria and progressive CKD, sensorineural deafness, lenticonus
tm.g: Kidney + ears + eyes with X-linked inheritance = type IV collagen (Alport)
f: he had tall stature and upward lens dislocation
he had huge cystic kidneys and a berry aneurysm in his 40s
he had gout and shrunken kidneys with a dominant family history
he had a Wilms tumour with aniridia as a child
x: Marfan syndrome, with lens dislocation and aortic root disease
ADPKD, with enlarged cystic kidneys in adults
A cause of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial disease with gout
Wilms tumour syndromes, not deafness and lenticonus

q.s: A 52-year-old woman has 3 weeks of sinus pain with bloody nasal discharge, cough, and blood-tinged sputum. Chest CT shows multiple cavitating nodules. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts, and serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. Kidney biopsy shows crescents with little or no immunoglobulin or complement on immunofluorescence.
q.w: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects the upper airway, lungs and kidneys with necrotising granulomas and a pauci-immune crescentic GN. PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is typical. MPO-ANCA fits microscopic polyangiitis (no granulomas, no upper airway disease) and eosinophilic granulomatosis.
q.f: No sinus disease and no granulomas → anti-myeloperoxidase (microscopic polyangiitis)
q.ql: Which of the following antibodies is most likely present?

c: little or no immunoglobulin or complement
tm.m: PR3-ANCA activate primed neutrophils → necrotising vasculitis of small vessels → granulomas in airways, crescents in glomeruli → haemoptysis, sinusitis, RPGN
tm.g: Sinuses + lungs + kidneys + pauci-immune crescents = GPA (PR3)
f: she had a malar rash and wire loops on biopsy
biopsy had shown linear IgG staining
she had kidney and lung involvement but no sinus disease or granulomas
she had nephrotic syndrome with spike and dome basement membrane
x: Lupus nephritis shows granular immune deposits
Gives linear IgG, not pauci-immune staining
Microscopic polyangiitis spares the sinuses and lacks granulomas
Membranous nephropathy is nephrotic

q.s: A 4-year-old boy has swelling around his eyes for 1 week that started after a cold. His legs are now swollen. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL, and serum cholesterol is high.
o: Normal light microscopy with effacement of podocyte foot processes
q.w: Minimal change disease is the commonest nephrotic syndrome in children. Light microscopy looks normal; electron microscopy shows effaced podocyte foot processes. Loss of the charge barrier leaks albumin selectively, and nearly all children respond to corticosteroids, so biopsy is often skipped.
q.f: An adult with anti-PLA2R antibodies → subepithelial spikes with granular IgG
q.ql: Which of the following findings is most likely on kidney biopsy?

tm.m: Cytokines from T cells injure podocytes → foot processes efface → charge barrier lost → selective albuminuria → low oncotic pressure → oedema; liver makes more lipoproteins
tm.g: Child + pure nephrotic + after a cold = minimal change; light microscopy is normal
f: his creatinine had tripled in 2 weeks with haematuria
he had haematuria 2 days after a cold with normal complement
he had long-standing diabetes with proteinuria
he had been a 50-year-old with anti-PLA2R antibodies
x: Rapidly progressive GN is nephritic
IgA nephropathy presents with haematuria
Diabetic nephropathy after years of diabetes
Membranous nephropathy in adults

q.s: A 56-year-old man has 2 months of leg swelling and frothy urine. He takes no medications. Urine protein is 6.2 g/24 h, and urinalysis shows no red blood cells. Serum albumin is 2.3 g/dL. Serum antibodies against a podocyte transmembrane receptor are positive. Biopsy shows thickened capillary walls without cell proliferation.
o: Foot process effacement with normal capillary walls
Spike and dome appearance on silver stain
Tram-track double contour of the basement membrane
q.w: Membranous nephropathy is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. Antibodies to the phospholipase A₂ receptor on podocytes form subepithelial immune deposits; new basement membrane grows between them, giving spikes on silver stain. Secondary forms follow SLE, hepatitis B, NSAIDs and solid tumours.
q.f: Hepatitis C with low C3 and a nephritic picture → tram-track double contour
q.ql: Which additional finding is most likely on the biopsy?

tm.m: Anti-PLA2R binds podocytes → subepithelial immune complexes → complement injures podocytes → heavy proteinuria; basement membrane grows around deposits → spike and dome
tm.g: Adult nephrotic + anti-PLA2R + thick capillary walls = membranous, spike and dome
f: his creatinine had tripled in weeks with haematuria
he had been a child with normal light microscopy
he had haematuria after a cold with normal complement
he had hepatitis C, low C3 and haematuria
x: Rapidly progressive GN, which is nephritic
Minimal change disease
IgA nephropathy, which is nephritic
Membranoproliferative GN

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 14 years has a urine albumin to creatinine ratio of 410 mg/g. Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. She is started on lisinopril.
q.w: In diabetic nephropathy, glomerular hyperfiltration (partly from efferent arteriole hyalinosis and angiotensin II) drives damage. ACE inhibitors relax the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. Expect a small, acceptable rise in creatinine.
q.f: The drug had been an SGLT2 inhibitor → increased renal tubular glucose excretion
q.ql: The drug slows progression of her kidney disease mainly through which of the following?

c: albumin to creatinine ratio of 410 mg/g
tm.m: Angiotensin II squeezes the efferent arteriole → high glomerular pressure → hyperfiltration injury → ACE inhibitor relaxes efferent → pressure and proteinuria fall
tm.g: ACE inhibitors protect diabetic kidneys by opening the efferent arteriole
f: the question asked about prostaglandins that NSAIDs block
the question asked what angiotensin II does in the glomerulus
the drug had been empagliflozin and the question asked about urine glucose
the question asked about collapsing FSGS in HIV
x: Would raise glomerular pressure; prostaglandins do this
That is the harm being reversed
SGLT2 inhibitors, not ACE inhibitors
Not how ACE inhibitors work

q.s: A 61-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has leg swelling and frothy urine. Urine protein is 5.8 g/24 h. Abdominal fat pad aspirate stained with Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
q.w: Chronic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infection) keeps the liver making serum amyloid A, an acute-phase protein that deposits as AA amyloid. Kidneys are the commonest target, giving nephrotic syndrome. AL amyloid from light chains fits myeloma.
q.f: Same biopsy with a monoclonal protein and no inflammation → immunoglobulin light chains
q.ql: The deposited protein is most likely derived from which of the following?

tm.m: Chronic inflammation → IL-6 → liver makes serum amyloid A → misfolded fragments form β-pleated sheets → deposit in glomeruli → nephrotic syndrome
tm.g: Amyloid + chronic inflammation = AA (serum amyloid A)
f: she had a monoclonal spike and no inflammatory disease
the question asked about pancreatic islet deposits in type 2 diabetes
she had restrictive cardiomyopathy in old age with a normal kidney
she had been on haemodialysis for 15 years with carpal tunnel syndrome
x: AL amyloid with plasma cell disorders
Deposits in islets in type 2 diabetes
Senile cardiac or hereditary amyloid
Deposits in long-term dialysis patients

q.s: A 74-year-old man has had 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea with poor oral intake. He is lightheaded on standing. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. The urine is concentrated, and microscopy shows a few hyaline casts.
q.w: FENa = (urine Na × plasma creatinine) ÷ (plasma Na × urine creatinine) × 100 = (10 × 2.0) ÷ (138 × 120) × 100, about 0.12%. Under 1% with BUN to creatinine of 32 means the tubules are working hard to hold sodium: prerenal azotaemia from volume loss.
q.f: Muddy brown casts with FENa over 2% → acute tubular necrosis
q.ql: Which of the following best fits his fractional excretion of sodium and diagnosis?

tm.m: Volume loss → low renal perfusion → aldosterone and ADH up → tubules reclaim Na⁺ and urea avidly → FENa under 1%, BUN to creatinine over 20
tm.g: FENa under 1% plus BUN to creatinine over 20 = prerenal
f: he had a palpable bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis early on
he had fever, rash and urine eosinophils after a new antibiotic
urine sodium had been 60 with muddy brown granular casts
he had been given furosemide the night before, which raises FENa despite low perfusion
x: Early obstruction can look prerenal, but nothing suggests obstruction here
Needs a drug trigger and WBC casts
The tubules here still conserve sodium
Only fits a prerenal patient on a diuretic; his FENa is 0.12%

q.s: A 66-year-old man is hospitalized for an infection of a prosthetic knee and treated with intravenous gentamicin and vancomycin. On day 8, his serum creatinine rises from 1.0 mg/dL to 2.8 mg/dL. He has no rash or fever. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts, and fractional excretion of sodium is 3.2%.
q.w: Aminoglycosides are taken up by proximal tubule cells through megalin and injure them, causing acute tubular necrosis after 5 to 10 days of therapy. Dead cells slough into the lumen and form muddy brown granular casts, and the injured tubule cannot reclaim sodium (FENa over 2%).
q.f: Fever, rash and eosinophils in the urine → interstitium with eosinophils
q.ql: Which part of the nephron is most likely injured?

tm.m: Aminoglycoside filtered → endocytosed by PCT cells → lysosomal and mitochondrial injury → cells necrose and slough → casts block tubules → GFR falls, sodium wasted
tm.g: Aminoglycoside + muddy brown casts + FENa over 2% = proximal tubular ATN
f: he had developed polyuria with dilute urine on lithium
he had haemoptysis and RBC casts
he had developed fever, rash and eosinophiluria
he had sickle cell trait with gross haematuria and flank pain
x: Lithium affects it, causing nephrogenic DI rather than ATN
Glomerular injury gives RBC casts
Acute interstitial nephritis gives WBC casts and often rash
Papillary necrosis presents with haematuria and colic

q.s: A 47-year-old woman develops fever and a pruritic, maculopapular rash 10 days after starting omeprazole for heartburn. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 mg/dL to 2.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows white blood cell casts and sterile pyuria. Peripheral eosinophil count is elevated.
o: T cell-mediated hypersensitivity in the interstitium
q.w: Acute interstitial nephritis is a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, typically to PPIs, penicillins, NSAIDs or diuretics. Fever, rash, eosinophilia and WBC casts with sterile pyuria are the clues. Stopping the drug is the key step; steroids may help.
q.f: Haematuria with linear IgG → antibody against type IV collagen
q.ql: Which of the following best describes the kidney injury?

c: fever and a pruritic, maculopapular rash
tm.m: Drug acts as a hapten on tubular proteins → T cells and eosinophils infiltrate the interstitium → tubules swell and fail → creatinine rises, WBC casts appear
tm.g: New drug + fever + rash + eosinophils + WBC casts = AIN, a type IV reaction
f: she had haemoptysis and linear IgG on biopsy
she had high-dose acyclovir without fluids
she had hypotension from sepsis with muddy brown casts
she had schistocytes and low platelets after bloody diarrhoea
x: Anti-GBM disease causes RBC casts
Acyclovir, methotrexate or ethylene glycol
ATN gives muddy brown casts, without rash or eosinophilia
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome with schistocytes

q.s: A 23-year-old Black man with sickle cell trait has sudden painless gross hematuria after a week of marathon training. He takes ibuprofen frequently for leg pain. Urine culture is negative. CT urography shows a ring-shaped filling defect at the tip of a renal pyramid.
o: Ischemic necrosis of the renal papilla
Sloughed tumor from the renal pelvis
q.w: The renal medulla is hypoxic and hypertonic; in sickle cell trait, red cells sickle in the vasa recta and starve the papillae, especially with dehydration and NSAIDs. The papilla dies and sloughs, causing gross haematuria and sometimes colic. Other causes: analgesics, diabetes, acute pyelonephritis.
q.f: Haematuria with oedema and heavy proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome → thrombosis of the renal vein
q.ql: Which of the following best explains his condition?

tm.m: Hypoxic, hypertonic medulla → red cells sickle in the vasa recta (plus NSAIDs remove prostaglandin dilation) → papillary ischaemia → necrosis and sloughing → gross haematuria
tm.g: Sickle trait + NSAIDs + haematuria from the papilla = papillary necrosis
f: he had cola urine 3 weeks after strep throat
he had intermittent flank pain after heavy drinking since childhood
he had been a smoker in his 60s with a filling defect in the renal pelvis
he had nephrotic syndrome with sudden flank pain
x: Would give RBC casts and proteinuria
Causes hydronephrosis, not a papillary defect
Urothelial cancer in an older smoker
Complicates nephrotic syndrome

q.s: A 59-year-old man with chronic kidney disease from long-standing hypertension has aching bone pain in his hips and legs and generalized itching. His estimated GFR is 18 mL/min/1.73 m². He is not yet on dialysis and takes amlodipine and furosemide. Hand x-rays show subperiosteal bone resorption.
q.w: Failing kidneys retain phosphate, which binds calcium and drives FGF23; FGF23 and the loss of renal mass cut 1α-hydroxylase, so calcitriol falls and gut calcium absorption drops. Low calcium, high phosphate and low calcitriol all stimulate PTH: secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy.
q.f: Years later, calcium high and PTH very high → tertiary hyperparathyroidism (autonomous)
q.ql: Which of the following is the primary trigger for his hormonal abnormality?

tm.m: Nephron loss → phosphate retained, FGF23 up → calcitriol falls → calcium falls → parathyroid glands stimulated → PTH high → bone resorbed (osteitis fibrosa cystica)
tm.g: Low calcium + high phosphate + high PTH in CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism
f: calcium had been 11.4 with low phosphate and a neck mass
the question asked what loop diuretics do to calcium
calcium had been 13.5 with low PTH and a lung mass
calcium had been high with low PTH after megadoses of supplements
x: Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium
Failing kidneys excrete less, and this is not the trigger
Causes hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH
Causes hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH

q.s: A 64-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease from diabetes has 6 months of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She eats a varied diet and takes no iron supplements. She has had no bleeding, and a stool test for occult blood is negative. Peripheral smear shows normal-appearing red cells.
q.w: Erythropoietin comes from interstitial cells near the peritubular capillaries. As CKD destroys them, EPO falls, giving a normocytic, hypoproliferative anaemia with a low reticulocyte count. Iron stores here are adequate, so an EPO-stimulating agent is the treatment.
q.f: Low ferritin and microcytosis → iron deficiency
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anemia?

tm.m: CKD destroys peritubular interstitial cells → little EPO → marrow not stimulated → few reticulocytes → normocytic anaemia
tm.g: Normocytic, low reticulocytes, iron replete, CKD = low EPO
f: occult blood had been positive with low ferritin
MCV had been 112 fL with hypersegmented neutrophils
reticulocytes had been 6% with schistocytes
ferritin had been 8 ng/mL with an MCV of 72 fL
x: Would deplete iron and raise reticulocytes
Causes macrocytosis
Would raise reticulocytes
Ferritin is high and saturation normal

q.s: A 38-year-old woman with Crohn disease had 90 cm of ileum resected 3 years ago. She now has colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm radiopaque stone in the right ureter. Urine microscopy shows envelope-shaped crystals.
q.w: With ileal disease, unabsorbed fat binds calcium in the gut lumen. Oxalate normally pairs with that calcium and is excreted in stool; instead it stays free, is absorbed in the colon and is excreted in urine, forming calcium oxalate stones (enteric hyperoxaluria).
q.f: Hexagonal crystals in a young man → defective renal reabsorption of cystine
q.ql: Which of the following best explains her stone formation?

tm.m: Ileal loss → bile acids and fat malabsorbed → fat binds gut calcium → oxalate left free → colonic absorption → hyperoxaluria → calcium oxalate stones
tm.g: Fat malabsorption steals calcium from oxalate: enteric hyperoxaluria
f: urine had shown hexagonal crystals with a positive nitroprusside test
the stone had been radiolucent after chemotherapy for leukaemia
she had high calcium, high PTH and recurrent stones
she had a staghorn calculus with alkaline urine and Proteus
x: Cystinuria gives hexagonal crystals
Uric acid stones are radiolucent
Possible cause of calcium stones, but her bowel history explains these
Struvite stones with coffin-lid crystals

q.s: A 61-year-old woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has a large branching stone filling the left renal pelvis and calyces. Urine pH is 8.0, and microscopy shows coffin lid-shaped crystals. Urine smells of ammonia.
q.w: Urease splits urea into ammonia, alkalinising the urine. Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) then precipitates into staghorn calculi. Proteus mirabilis is the classic urease producer; Klebsiella and Staphylococcus saprophyticus can also make urease. The stone must be removed, because bacteria live inside it.
q.f: Radiolucent stone with acidic urine → uric acid, not infection
q.ql: Which organism most likely contributed to this stone?

tm.m: Urease → urea to ammonia → urine pH rises → struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) precipitates → staghorn calculus shelters bacteria → recurrent infection
tm.g: Alkaline urine + staghorn + coffin lids = urease (Proteus)
f: she had diabetes with fungal balls in the bladder
she had an infection after urinary catheterisation with a gram-positive coccus resistant to cephalosporins
the culture had grown a gram-negative rod that ferments lactose, with no stone
the infection had been in a pregnant woman screened for group B strep
x: Causes fungal UTI and fungus balls, not struvite
Not a typical urease producer
The commonest UTI cause, but it does not make urease
Not a urease producer

q.s: A 58-year-old man starts chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia with a white blood cell count of 160,000/mm³. Two days later his urine output falls and his creatinine rises. Serum potassium is 6.1 mEq/L, phosphate is 7.8 mg/dL, and uric acid is 15 mg/dL. Plain x-ray shows no stones, but ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis.
q.w: Tumour lysis releases nucleic acids that are broken down to uric acid, which crystallises in acidic tubular fluid and forms radiolucent stones (invisible on plain film). Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and lowers uric acid production; rasburicase breaks down uric acid already formed. Hydration comes first.
q.f: Uric acid already formed and needing breakdown → rasburicase
q.ql: Which drug given before chemotherapy would have most directly prevented this complication by lowering uric acid production?

tm.m: Chemotherapy lyses blasts → purines released → xanthine oxidase makes uric acid → crystals in acidic collecting ducts → obstructive uropathy
tm.g: Prevent tumour lysis: fluids plus a xanthine oxidase inhibitor
f: the question asked about an acute gout flare to be settled fast
the question asked about calcium stones that recur with hypercalciuria
the question asked about raising uric acid excretion in gout with low urate output
the question asked how to dissolve an existing uric acid stone
x: Treats gout inflammation; it does not lower uric acid
Lowers urine calcium and can raise serum urate
Increases urate excretion, which raises tubular uric acid and worsens tumour lysis
Alkalinisation is no longer routine and does not reduce production

q.s: A 15-year-old boy has had three episodes of kidney stones since age 10. His older sister also has recurrent stones. Urine microscopy shows flat hexagonal crystals, and the urinary cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive.
q.w: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of the PCT transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine (COLA). Cystine is poorly soluble and forms hexagonal crystals and stones from childhood. Treatment: lots of fluid, urine alkalinisation and chelators such as penicillamine or tiopronin.
q.f: Pellagra-like rash with aminoaciduria → neutral amino acids including tryptophan (Hartnup)
q.ql: A defect in the renal reabsorption of which group of amino acids is most likely?

tm.m: Transporter for dibasic amino acids and cystine fails in the PCT → cystine filtered but not reclaimed → poorly soluble cystine in urine → hexagonal crystals → stones
tm.g: Hexagonal crystals + positive nitroprusside = cystinuria (COLA)
f: he had urine that smelt of maple syrup in infancy
he had iminoglycinuria found on newborn screening
he had a pellagra-like rash with ataxia
he had a musty odour, fair skin and intellectual disability
x: Maple syrup urine disease is a metabolic, not transport, defect
Iminoglycinuria is benign and does not cause stones
Hartnup disease, which causes pellagra-like features
Phenylketonuria, a liver enzyme defect

q.s: A 42-year-old man has sudden, severe headache followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. He has had hypertension and intermittent flank pain for years, and his father died on dialysis. Both kidneys are palpable. CT of the head shows blood in the subarachnoid space.
q.w: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is usually a PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16 (PKD2 on chromosome 4 is milder). Huge cystic kidneys bring hypertension, haematuria, stones and CKD; berry aneurysms can rupture as subarachnoid haemorrhage. Liver cysts, mitral valve prolapse and diverticulosis also occur.
q.f: A newborn with Potter sequence and liver fibrosis → chromosome 6 (PKHD1)
q.ql: A mutation in a gene on which chromosome is most likely responsible for his kidney disease?

tm.m: PKD1 mutation → polycystin fails → tubular cells proliferate into cysts → kidneys enlarge, RAAS activated → hypertension; vessel wall defect → berry aneurysm → subarachnoid haemorrhage
tm.g: Big cystic kidneys + family history + berry aneurysm = ADPKD, chromosome 16
f: he had renal cell carcinoma, retinal haemangioblastomas and cerebellar tumours
he had been a newborn with Potter sequence and congenital hepatic fibrosis
he had been a toddler with a flank mass and aniridia
he had haematuria with deafness and lenticonus
x: VHL gene, with renal cell carcinoma and haemangioblastomas
PKHD1 in autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
WT1 in Wilms tumour
Alport syndrome, usually X-linked

q.s: A newborn girl has respiratory distress shortly after birth. Her mother had oligohydramnios. The baby has a flattened nose, recessed chin, and low-set ears. Both flanks are distended by enormous, smooth kidneys. Liver ultrasonography shows periportal fibrosis.
q.w: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (PKHD1, fibrocystin) presents in infancy with huge spongy kidneys, oligohydramnios and Potter sequence; pulmonary hypoplasia causes the respiratory distress. Congenital hepatic fibrosis leads to portal hypertension in survivors.
q.f: Adult with berry aneurysm and cystic kidneys → autosomal dominant
q.ql: Which of the following best describes the inheritance of this condition?

tm.m: PKHD1 mutation → collecting duct cysts in utero → no fetal urine → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence and pulmonary hypoplasia; bile duct plate fails → hepatic fibrosis
tm.g: Newborn with huge kidneys + liver fibrosis + Potter = ARPKD
f: she had been an adult with cystic kidneys and a family history in her father
she had lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes and ragged red fibres
she had cleft lip and palate with no family history
she had hypophosphataemic rickets like her father
x: ADPKD usually presents in adults
Fits MELAS-type diseases, not cystic kidneys
Cleft lip or neural tube defects
Hypophosphataemic rickets and Rett syndrome

q.s: A 63-year-old man who smokes has 2 months of dull left flank pain and visible hematuria. He has also noticed a new swelling of veins in his left scrotum that does not drain when he lies down. Hemoglobin is 19.2 g/dL. CT shows a 7-cm mass in the left kidney extending into the renal vein.
o: Urothelial cells of the renal pelvis
q.w: Renal cell carcinoma arises from proximal tubule cells; the clear cell type follows VHL loss on chromosome 3, which stabilises HIF and drives VEGF and EPO. EPO causes polycythaemia. The tumour grows into the renal vein; on the left this blocks the gonadal vein and causes a varicocele that does not empty on lying down.
q.f: A benign tumour with a central scar and mitochondria-packed cells → collecting duct intercalated cells (oncocytoma)
q.ql: The tumor most likely arises from which of the following cells?

c: does not drain when he lies down
tm.m: VHL lost → HIF accumulates → VEGF and EPO switched on → vascular tumour invades the renal vein → left gonadal vein blocked → varicocele; EPO → polycythaemia
tm.g: Flank mass + haematuria + polycythaemia + left varicocele = RCC from proximal tubule cells
f: biopsy had shown large eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria and a central scar
he had a young patient's hypertension with high renin and a small kidney tumour
he had been a 3-year-old with a flank mass
he had painless haematuria with a filling defect in the pelvis after aniline dye work
x: Oncocytoma, usually benign
Reninoma, a rare cause of hypertension
Wilms tumour in young children
Urothelial carcinoma, without polycythaemia

q.s: A 3-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of a firm, smooth mass in the right flank found while bathing. It does not cross the midline. She has hypertension and microscopic hematuria. She also has enlargement of the right arm and leg compared with the left, and she had an umbilical defect repaired at birth.
q.w: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the commonest kidney cancer in children aged 2 to 4: a smooth unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline, with haematuria and renin-driven hypertension. Hemihypertrophy and an omphalocele point to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (WT2 region on chromosome 11).
q.f: A mass crossing the midline with raised catecholamines → neuroblastoma
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

c: enlargement of the right arm and leg
tm.m: Loss of WT1 or WT2 on chromosome 11 → embryonic kidney tissue keeps proliferating → mass of blastema, stroma and epithelium → renin release → hypertension
tm.g: Child + flank mass not crossing midline + hemihypertrophy = Wilms (Beckwith-Wiedemann)
f: the mass had come from the liver with a very high AFP
the mass had crossed the midline with high urine homovanillic acid
he had been a 60-year-old smoker with polycythaemia
the mass had been in the sacrococcygeal region with teeth and hair
x: Arises in the liver, with a high AFP
Often crosses the midline and raises catecholamine metabolites
A disease of older adults
Contains tissue from all three germ layers, usually sacrococcygeal in infants

q.s: A 64-year-old man who worked for 30 years in a dye manufacturing plant has painless gross hematuria. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 40 years. Cystoscopy shows a papillary mass on the bladder wall.
q.w: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma is the commonest bladder cancer. Risk factors: smoking, aromatic amines in dye and rubber work, phenacetin and cyclophosphamide. Painless haematuria in an older smoker is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. Squamous cell carcinoma follows Schistosoma haematobium and chronic irritation.
q.f: Bladder cancer in an Egyptian farmer with schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma
q.ql: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

c: smoked a pack of cigarettes a day
tm.m: Aromatic amines and tobacco carcinogens filtered → concentrated in urine → contact with urothelium → DNA damage → papillary urothelial carcinoma
tm.g: Painless haematuria + smoking + dye work = urothelial carcinoma
f: the tumour had been at the bladder dome in the midline
the tumour had been a bulky smooth muscle tumour after pelvic radiation
he had a flank mass with polycythaemia
he had grown up with schistosomiasis in Egypt
x: Rare, at the dome, from urachal remnants
Rare smooth muscle cancer
A kidney tumour with a different risk profile
Linked to schistosomiasis and chronic irritation

q.s: A healthy 25-year-old volunteer takes part in a physiology study of kidney function. He receives a continuous infusion of inulin and para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) until plasma levels are stable. After equilibration, a timed urine collection and a midpoint plasma sample are obtained. He has normal blood pressure and takes no medications.
q.w: GFR is inulin clearance: 100 × 1.2 ÷ 1 = 120 mL/min. Effective renal plasma flow is PAH clearance: 1000 × 1.2 ÷ 2 = 600 mL/min. Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ RPF = 120 ÷ 600 = 20%.
q.f: Efferent arteriole constricted by angiotensin II → filtration fraction above 20%
q.ql: Which of the following is closest to this volunteer's filtration fraction?

tm.m: Inulin filtered only → clearance = GFR; PAH filtered and secreted → clearance = RPF → divide one by the other
tm.g: FF = C inulin ÷ C PAH
f: GFR had been 60 with an RPF of 600
GFR had been 90 with an RPF of 600
GFR had been 120 with an RPF of 480
the PAH clearance had been mistaken for renal blood flow at a GFR of 300
x: Would need a GFR of 60
Would need a GFR of 90
Would need an RPF of 480
Uses the wrong numerator or denominator

q.s: A 71-year-old woman with heart failure and chronic kidney disease takes furosemide and lisinopril. She develops knee osteoarthritis and starts taking naproxen daily. Two weeks later her serum creatinine has risen from 1.4 mg/dL to 2.6 mg/dL and her ankles are more swollen.
o: Afferent constriction with decreased GFR and RPF
Efferent constriction with increased filtration fraction
q.w: In heart failure and CKD, renal perfusion leans on prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole, and on angiotensin II at the efferent arteriole. Naproxen removes the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and both RPF and GFR fall. With an ACE inhibitor already relaxing the efferent arteriole, GFR collapses.
q.f: Starting lisinopril alone → efferent dilation with decreased GFR
q.ql: Which of the following best describes the change in her glomerular hemodynamics caused by the new drug?

tm.m: NSAID → prostaglandin synthesis blocked → afferent arteriole constricts → less flow into the glomerulus → RPF and GFR fall → creatinine rises, salt retained → oedema
tm.g: NSAIDs squeeze the afferent; ACE inhibitors relax the efferent; together they crush GFR
f: she had been a pregnant woman in the second trimester
she had been given angiotensin II in shock
the new drug had been lisinopril itself
she had a stone obstructing the ureter
x: The opposite of an NSAID effect; pregnancy does this
Angiotensin II, not an NSAID
The ACE inhibitor's effect, which she already had
Postrenal obstruction

q.s: A 30-year-old woman in the second trimester of pregnancy has glucose detected on a routine urine dipstick. Her fasting plasma glucose is 82 mg/dL, and a glucose tolerance test is normal. She has no polyuria or thirst.
o: Defective insulin secretion from beta cells
Increased filtered load of glucose with a lowered reabsorptive threshold
Mutation in the SGLT1 transporter of the small intestine
Proximal tubular damage from Fanconi syndrome
q.w: Pregnancy raises GFR by up to about 50%, so more glucose is filtered per minute, and proximal reabsorption becomes less efficient. Some glucose escapes into the urine although plasma glucose and glucose tolerance are normal: benign glucosuria of pregnancy.
q.f: Abnormal glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks → gestational diabetes mellitus
q.ql: Which of the following best explains her glucosuria?

tm.m: Pregnancy → GFR up → more glucose filtered → SGLT2 capacity exceeded at a lower plasma level → glucose spills into urine
tm.g: Glucosuria with normal blood glucose in pregnancy = physiological, from a higher GFR
f: she had been a thin teenager with ketoacidosis and very high glucose
her glucose tolerance test had been abnormal
she had been a newborn with severe watery diarrhoea from glucose and galactose
she had aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and a normal anion gap acidosis
x: Type 1 diabetes would raise plasma glucose
Her glucose tolerance test is normal
Causes glucose-galactose malabsorption in infants
Would cause other losses and acidosis

q.s: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes is started on a new antihypertensive drug. Two weeks later, he presents with swelling of the lips and tongue but no hives or itching. He has no history of allergies. Serum potassium is 5.4 mEq/L.
q.w: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which also degrades bradykinin. Bradykinin builds up, causing vasodilation and vascular leak: angioedema without urticaria, and a dry cough. The same drug lowers aldosterone, explaining the raised potassium. An ARB is usually substituted, with care.
q.f: Swelling with hives and itching after peanuts → histamine
q.ql: Accumulation of which of the following most likely caused his swelling?

c: swelling of the lips and tongue but no hives or itching
tm.m: ACE inhibitor → ACE blocked → bradykinin not degraded → vasodilation and capillary leak → angioedema; less angiotensin II → less aldosterone → K⁺ retained
tm.g: Angioedema without hives on an ACE inhibitor = bradykinin
f: the question asked which hormone constricts the efferent arteriole
he had urticaria and wheeze after eating peanuts
he had asthma worsened by aspirin with nasal polyps
the question asked what rises in plasma when ACE is blocked, upstream of the block
x: Falls with an ACE inhibitor
Causes urticaria and itch, which he lacks
Drives aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
Rises as feedback, but renin does not cause angioedema

q.s: A 15-year-old girl with short stature, a webbed neck, and widely spaced nipples has an abdominal ultrasound for recurrent urinary tract infections. Both kidneys are joined at their lower poles and lie lower than normal in the abdomen.
q.w: In horseshoe kidney the lower poles fuse, and the isthmus catches under the inferior mesenteric artery as the kidneys ascend from the pelvis. It is associated with Turner syndrome and trisomies. Most are asymptomatic, but obstruction, stones, infection and Wilms tumour are more common.
q.f: A left renal vein compressed during development → superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker)
q.ql: Ascent of the fused kidney was most likely blocked by which of the following?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal hysterectomy for large fibroids. On the second postoperative day she has right flank pain and fever, and a CT scan shows right hydroureteronephrosis with abrupt narrowing of the distal ureter near the cervix.
o: Ovarian artery in the suspensory ligament
q.w: Near the cervix the ureter passes just beneath the uterine artery (water under the bridge), so clamping or ligating the uterine artery can catch it. The ovarian vessels in the suspensory ligament are a second danger point, but higher, at the pelvic brim.
q.f: Injury at the pelvic brim while dividing the infundibulopelvic ligament → ovarian artery
q.ql: During the operation, the ureter was most likely injured while ligating which of the following?

c: abrupt narrowing of the distal ureter near the cervix
tm.m: Ureter runs under the uterine artery 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix → clamp placed on the artery catches the ureter → obstruction → hydronephrosis and flank pain
tm.g: Water under the bridge: the ureter lies beneath the uterine artery
f: the bleeding had come from the lower anterior abdominal wall during port placement
the narrowing had been at the pelvic brim near the ovarian vessels
the question asked what runs through the inguinal canal in a woman
the injury had been during closure of the vaginal cuff
x: Lies in the anterior abdominal wall
A danger point, but at the pelvic brim, not beside the cervix
Runs to the inguinal canal, away from the ureter
Below the level where the ureter crosses

q.s: A 20-year-old sexually active woman has 2 days of burning on urination and urinary frequency. She is afebrile. Urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase but is nitrite negative. Urine culture grows a gram-positive coccus in clusters that is catalase positive, coagulase negative, and resistant to novobiocin.
q.w: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is the second commonest cause of cystitis in young sexually active women. It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is novobiocin resistant (S. epidermidis is sensitive). Gram-positive organisms do not reduce nitrate, so the nitrite test is negative.
q.f: Novobiocin sensitive on a prosthetic valve → Staphylococcus epidermidis
q.ql: Which of the following organisms is most likely?

tm.m: Gram-positive cocci in clusters → catalase positive (staphylococcus) → coagulase negative → novobiocin resistant → S. saprophyticus
tm.g: Coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staph in a young woman's cystitis = saprophyticus
f: the isolate had been catalase-negative cocci in chains growing in 6.5% salt
the isolate had been coagulase positive
the isolate had been novobiocin sensitive from an infected catheter
the isolate had been a catalase-negative, beta-haemolytic, CAMP-positive coccus in pregnancy
x: Catalase negative cocci in chains
Coagulase positive
Novobiocin sensitive; infects catheters and prostheses
Catalase negative, in chains

q.s: A 6-year-old girl has had five episodes of febrile urinary tract infection. A voiding cystourethrogram shows contrast flowing back from the bladder into both ureters and renal pelves. Her blood pressure is high for her age.
o: Foamy lipid-laden macrophages around a staghorn stone
Muddy brown granular casts in tubules
Scarring with dilated tubules containing eosinophilic casts
q.w: Vesicoureteral reflux lets infected urine reach the kidneys repeatedly, producing chronic pyelonephritis: coarse corticomedullary scars, blunted calyces and atrophic, dilated tubules filled with eosinophilic casts that resemble thyroid follicles (thyroidisation). Scarring causes hypertension and CKD.
q.f: A staghorn Proteus stone with foamy macrophages → xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
q.ql: Biopsy of her kidneys would most likely show which of the following?

c: five episodes of febrile urinary tract infection
flowing back from the bladder into both ureters
tm.m: Reflux → infected urine reaches the papillae → repeated pyelonephritis → scarring and tubular atrophy → thyroid-like tubules with casts → renin up and nephrons lost → hypertension and CKD
tm.g: Repeated infection plus reflux = chronic pyelonephritis with thyroidisation
f: her creatinine had tripled in 2 weeks with RBC casts
she had a staghorn calculus with Proteus infection
she had received aminoglycosides for 10 days
she had been nephrotic after a cold
x: Rapidly progressive GN
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
Acute tubular necrosis
Minimal change disease

q.s: A 29-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation has severe preeclampsia and receives an intravenous infusion to prevent seizures. Six hours later she is drowsy, and her respirations are 8/min. Deep tendon reflexes cannot be elicited.
q.w: Magnesium sulfate toxicity first abolishes deep tendon reflexes, then depresses breathing and finally the heart. Calcium gluconate antagonises magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and cardiac membrane, reversing it quickly; the infusion is stopped.
q.f: Pinpoint pupils after an opioid → naloxone
q.ql: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

c: Deep tendon reflexes cannot be elicited
tm.m: Magnesium sulfate → blocks calcium entry and acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction → reflexes lost → respiratory muscles weaken → calcium competes and restores release
tm.g: Lost reflexes on a magnesium infusion = magnesium toxicity: give calcium
f: she had become drowsy after midazolam
her blood pressure had been 180/120 mm Hg with normal reflexes
she had pinpoint pupils after morphine for pain
she had dry skin, dilated pupils and delirium after an antihistamine overdose
x: Reverses benzodiazepines
Treats severe hypertension but not magnesium toxicity
Reverses opioids
Reverses anticholinergic toxicity

q.s: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted at a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m². Nasogastric feeding at full calories is started. On day 3 she becomes breathless and confused, with ankle edema and an irregular pulse.
o: Insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, causing ATP depletion
q.w: Refeeding switches metabolism from fat back to carbohydrate. Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, and total body phosphate was already depleted, so ATP and 2,3-BPG production fail: heart failure, respiratory muscle weakness, arrhythmias, confusion and rhabdomyolysis. Feeding should start low and rise slowly, with electrolytes replaced.
q.f: Ataxia and ophthalmoplegia after glucose without thiamine → thiamine deficiency (not excess)
q.ql: Which of the following best explains her deterioration?

tm.m: Carbohydrate load → insulin surge → phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ pulled into cells → depleted phosphate stores collapse → no ATP for heart and diaphragm → heart failure and arrhythmia
tm.g: Refeeding syndrome kills through low phosphate: start feeds slowly
f: she had been bedbound with a high calcium and a fracture
her glucose had been 600 with polyuria
the question had been about high-dose vitamin supplements causing harm
her sodium had been 118 after drinking large volumes of water
x: Her problem is low phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Glucose is only mildly raised
Thiamine excess is not harmful; deficiency is the risk
Sodium is not given as low here
